A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VPI-Bench. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised, and added material.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of seven agents, behavioral and injection-timing analyses, defense experiments, and human-validated LLM-judge results.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds GPT-5 evaluations, UI-TARS results in Appendix G, and the Email task comparison in Section 4.7.

M1.justification: The visual-injection construction, sandboxed interactions, and three-LLM majority-vote evaluation pipeline remain unchanged. Additional threat-model explanations do not establish a new attack algorithm. The independent action guard discussed in v2 is a future direction, not an implemented component.

E1.justification: Both versions use 306 cases across the same five platforms, comprising 219 Computer-Use and 87 Browser-Use cases. Replying to and summarizing emails already appear in v1's task breakdown; v2's comparison analyzes existing coverage. Expanded task descriptions and interface illustrations do not establish additional scenarios.

E2.justification: V2 adds GPT-5 to the Browser-Use comparison in Table 1 and evaluates UI-TARS-7B on Amazon and Messenger in Appendix G. The seven original agents remain. The expanded discussion of fine-tuning and framework defenses does not introduce separately evaluated defense baselines.

E3.justification: The reported system-defense condition changes from v1's short warning in Section 4.6 to the longer intent-alignment and privacy instructions in v2 Appendix D. This establishes a reported protocol revision without proving that experiments were rerun. V2 also adds task-stratified Email analysis and UI-TARS-7B evaluation; the primary metrics and judging procedure remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.7 adds a focused analysis of semantic relatedness using Email reply versus summary tasks. Appendix G adds UI-TARS failure analysis, including hallucinated interface elements and a message-handling example. The existing Sonnet behavioral and injection-timing analyses remain, while the system-defense analysis receives revised results.

E5.justification: Table 1 newly reports standard deviations alongside the mean attempted and success rates. Both versions specify three independent runs, so this is additional uncertainty reporting rather than evidence of increased replication. No new confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: V2 substantially expands and revises reported outcomes: GPT-5 results, UI-TARS attempted rates of 78.95%/70% with zero success on Amazon/Messenger, and Email reply/summary attempted rates of 96.67%/16.67%. Many Figure 5 defended-condition values change under the revised reported prompt; Sonnet-3.7 CUA Amazon AR/SR changes from 45%/36% to 56%/42%. Table 1 changes Sonnet-3.7 BUA Messenger AR/SR from 23.08%/15.38% to 23.3%/16.7%. Figure 2 revises the combined unauthorized-action/privacy-leakage share from 25.5% to 54.9%. Most original undefended means remain equivalent after rounding.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 refines the threat assumptions: v2 explicitly permits attacker-controlled legitimate content without platform compromise and specifies no attacker knowledge of user tasks or agent architecture. V1 assumes a compromised page without these explicit information restrictions. The mathematical task relations and AR/SR definitions remain unchanged, with no new proofs.

C1.justification: V2 adds explicit claims about black-box attacks without knowledge of user tasks or agent architecture, and greater susceptibility when benign and malicious tasks are semantically related. The abstract broadens its defense statement beyond system prompts. The central benchmark contribution and high-vulnerability claims, including the 51%/100% maxima, remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds a contextual-plausibility explanation for the Email contrast and attributes UI-TARS failures to execution capacity rather than attack resistance. It also revises the defense discussion toward independent action guards. Appendix A removes the platform-diversity, advertisement-filtering, and simplified-webpage limitations, retaining human supervision. Together these substantially revise explanations and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: V2 adds a separate dataset link, web-platform code and deployment information, and a reproducibility statement. It further documents screenshot-based page construction, redirection to actual websites, the full revised defense prompt, and UI-TARS deployment/template choices. These disclosures do not establish that the original webpage implementation changed. Hardware, worker counts, and reported compute totals are retained.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to discuss AgentDojo, visual pop-up attacks, WebInject, UI-TARS, multimodal situational safety, and additional guard methods. A new defense subsection and explicit comparisons concerning attacker access, interaction depth, and downstream system harm materially broaden the positioning beyond v1's primarily HTML-focused account.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, threat-model discussion, and discussion/conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Agent-related-work subsections are merged, defense discussion is reorganized, publication and reproducibility/ethics/LLM-use statements are added, and appendices are expanded and relettered. These changes exceed the insertion of new scientific results.

P2.justification: V2 adopts the ICLR document layout and redistributes figures and tables. Table 1 changes from slash-separated rates to paired rows with uncertainty estimates; Table 2 gains a task-type column. Appendix I adds five interface screenshots as Figures 6–10. Figures 1, 3, and 4 retain their original graphical content.

improvement.justification: Standard deviations in Table 1, corrected task-goal accounting, clearer resource documentation, and focused additional evaluations improve transparency and empirical support. These gains are moderated by removal of three relevant applicability limitations and broad defense interpretations still based on different frameworks and task subsets. The net improvement is useful but limited; the core benchmark and principal conclusions remain intact.
